# Lecture 4: Conditioning, Bayes' rule, and independence {#b04} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 4, you can - calculate conditional probabilities and say which group each one refers to - rebuild an overall probability from the rates of separate groups - update a probability after new evidence with Bayes' rule - check whether two events are independent and tell this apart from disjoint ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

An investor who learns that a pitch is from a late season updates their expectations. A bank that sees a fraud warning on a payment does the same. Updating chances after new information is a core probability skill in business. It is also easy to turn the question around by mistake.

Late-season pitches reach deals more often. Two sentences about these pitches give the numbers 68.8% and 57.3%. What exactly does each sentence claim, and what does a positive flag from an AI tool that predicts deals really tell us? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Do all the preparation below before class.
Video preparation
Watch Conditional Probabilities and Bayes' Rule. Be ready to identify the reference class in a conditional probability and to explain why turning a condition around changes the denominator. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide. The videos explain key ideas in another way and can use a different notation. The lecture material and its notation always come first.
[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Warm up.** Lecture 2 built the counts table for deals and seasons from the Shark Tank file. Build it again. The events $D$ (on-air deal) and $L$ (late season) are defined as in Lecture 2: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 # on-air deal L <- sharks$season >= 9 # late season: Seasons 9-16 table(deal = D, late = L) ``` ::: Then compare, in words only: - "Among pitches in Seasons 9--16, what proportion reached an on-air deal?" - "Among pitches that reached an on-air deal, what proportion came from Seasons 9--16?" Both questions use the same cell of your table. Decide before class which part of the table each question looks at. **Predict.** Answer this question before you come to class. An AI classifier flags (marks) the pitches that are likely to get a deal. Of the pitches that it checks, only 10% reach a deal. The classifier flags 80% of the actual deals and also 20% of the non-deals. Of the flagged pitches, what share are deals: near 80%, near 50%, or near 30%? Choose one answer. You find the answer in the lecture material. If fractions or event notation are unfamiliar, review [Mathematics Refresher: sets and event notation](../resources/math-refresher.html#sets-and-event-notation) and [fractions and rearranging equations](../resources/math-refresher.html#fractions-and-rearranging-equations). ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## Lecture material This section starts from one counts table. On that table it builds four tools: conditional probability, the law of total probability, Bayes' rule, and independence of events. ### Start with a founder's question [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A founder hears that most deals on the show come from the later seasons. The founder concludes that a pitch in a later season is likely to end in a deal. Is that the same statement? Here are two sentences about the 1,441 pitches in the Shark Tank file: - **Sentence A.** "68.8% of late-season pitches reached an on-air deal." - **Sentence B.** "57.3% of the pitches that reached a deal came from the late seasons." Both sentences use the same 505 records: the late-season pitches that reached a deal. But they answer different questions and give different numbers. This lecture shows what each sentence claims. It also answers a harder question of the same kind: when an AI classifier flags a pitch as a likely deal, how much should that flag change what you believe? ### One table, five probabilities [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The starting point is the counts table from Lecture 2. The code builds the events $D$ (on-air deal, `deal_on_show`) and $L$ (late season, `season` 9 or higher) as before. Run it yourself: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 # on-air deal L <- sharks$season >= 9 # late season: Seasons 9-16 table(deal = D, late = L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` late deal FALSE TRUE FALSE 330 229 TRUE 377 505 ``` ::: ::: Written with row and column totals: | | Early ($L^c$, S1--8) | Late ($L$, S9--16) | Total | |--------------------|---------------------:|-------------------:|------:| | **No deal** ($D^c$) | 330 | 229 | **559** | | **Deal** ($D$) | 377 | 505 | **882** | | **Total** | **707** | **734** | **1441** | Each of the five quantities below is a fraction of two counts. Before you read on, find in the table the count that goes on top and the count that goes underneath. 1. $P(D)$, the probability that a pitch reached a deal. 2. $P(L)$, the probability that a pitch is from the late seasons. 3. $P(D\cap L)$, the probability that a pitch is from the late seasons and reached a deal. 4. Among late-season pitches, the share that reached a deal. 5. Among pitches that reached a deal, the share that came from the late seasons. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your denominators 1. $P(D)$: 882 deal records out of all 1,441 records. 2. $P(L)$: 734 late-season records out of all 1,441 records. 3. $P(D\cap L)$: 505 late-season deal records out of all 1,441 records. 4. Among late-season pitches, the share with a deal: 505 late-season deal records out of the 734 late-season records. 5. Among deal pitches, the share from the late seasons: 505 late-season deal records out of the 882 deal records. The first three all divide by 1,441, the number of all pitches. The last two divide by a part of the table. A share within a part of the table is called a conditional probability. The next section defines it. ::: ### Conditional probability

MIT explanation (review): 02.2 Conditional Probabilities.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Items 4 and 5 above ask the same kind of question: what is the probability of one event if you already know that another event happens? You answer both in two steps. First, keep only the pitches in one group. This group is called the **reference class**. Second, take the share of them in which the event happens. For item 4 the reference class is the 734 late-season pitches, and 505 of them reached a deal. Looking only at a reference class is called **conditioning** on it. The symbol for this is a vertical bar, read as "given". Item 4 is written $P(D\mid L)$, "the probability of $D$ given $L$". Item 5 is written $P(L\mid D)$. The event after the bar is always the reference class. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Conditional probability.** The probability that event $A$ happens, given that event $B$ happens. For events $A$ and $B$ with $P(B)>0$, $$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.$$ In words: keep only the outcomes in $B$, then take the share of them that are also in $A$. ::: The formula does the same two steps as the count. For item 4, $$P(D\mid L)=\frac{P(D\cap L)}{P(L)} =\frac{505/1441}{734/1441}=\frac{505}{734}.$$ The reference class gives the denominator. Dividing by $P(B)$ rescales the probabilities inside $B$ so that they add up to 1 again. For a fixed event $B$, conditional probabilities follow all three rules from Lecture 2. So every rule that Lecture 2 derived from them also holds inside the reference class. The condition is that the event after the bar stays the same in the whole calculation. Two examples follow. The first is the complement rule, $P(A^c\mid B)=1-P(A\mid B)$. Among late-season pitches, the share without a deal is $$P(D^c\mid L)=1-P(D\mid L)=1-\frac{505}{734}=\frac{229}{734}\approx 0.312.$$ The second is the addition rule. For two events $A$ and $C$ and the same reference class $B$, $$P(A\cup C\mid B)=P(A\mid B)+P(C\mid B)-P(A\cap C\mid B).$$ Some calculations mix different reference classes, for example $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(A\mid B^c)$. For these you need the law of total probability, which a later section explains. ::: {#exm-b04-conditional} ## Worked example: what each of the two sentences means [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Sentence A asks about $P(D\mid L)$.** Conditioning on $L$ means that you hide everything except the Late column: | | Early | **Late ($L$)** | |--------------------|------:|---------------:| | No deal | · | **229** | | Deal | · | **505** | | Total | · | **734** | Within that one column, 505 of 734 records are deals: $$P(D\mid L)=\frac{505}{734}\approx 0.688.$$ **Sentence B asks about $P(L\mid D)$.** Conditioning on $D$ means that you hide everything except the Deal row: | | Early | Late | Total | |--------------------|------:|-----:|------:| | No deal | · | · | · | | **Deal ($D$)** | **377** | **505** | **882** | Within that one row, 505 of 882 records are late-season: $$P(L\mid D)=\frac{505}{882}\approx 0.573.$$ The numerator is 505 in both calculations: the same cell of the table. The denominators differ, and so do the questions. Sentence A looks only at the 734 late-season pitches. Sentence B looks only at the 882 deal pitches. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: which sentence matches which number? Sentence A ("of late-season pitches, ... reached a deal") conditions on the season, so it is $P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 68.8\%$. Sentence B ("of deal pitches, ... came from late seasons") conditions on the deal, so it is $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 57.3\%$. A report that quotes "68.8% of deal pitches came from late seasons" has put the right number into the wrong sentence. ::: The same two numbers in R. `D[L]` keeps only the late-season pitches, and `L[D]` keeps only the deal pitches. This is the step that keeps only the reference class: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 c( P_deal_given_late = mean(D[L]), P_late_given_deal = mean(L[D]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` P_deal_given_late P_late_given_deal 0.6880109 0.5725624 ``` ::: ::: ### The multiplication rule

MIT explanation (review): 02.6 The Multiplication Rule.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The probability of an intersection, $P(A\cap B)$, is also called a **joint probability**: both events happen together. Multiply both sides of the definition of conditional probability by $P(B)$. The result is the **multiplication rule**. It builds a joint probability from a conditional one: $$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B).$$ The same holds with the roles of $A$ and $B$ exchanged, because $A\cap B$ and $B\cap A$ are the same event: $$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)=P(B\mid A)\,P(A).$$ This line explains why the two sentences share a numerator and have different denominators. Both products equal $505/1441$, but each one uses a different reference class. ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Try it: verify the joint probability two ways [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Try this first with the student next to you. Use the counts table to check the equation above for $D$ and $L$. *Step 1 (given).* The direct way: $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$. *Step 2 (given).* The first product: $P(D\mid L)\,P(L)=\dfrac{505}{734}\cdot\dfrac{734}{1441}$. The 734 cancels. Cancel it and confirm that $505/1441$ is left. *Step 3 (you).* Write the second product, $P(L\mid D)\,P(D)$, as two fractions from the table. Show that it also equals $505/1441$. *Step 4 (you).* Confirm all three ways in R. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer $P(L\mid D)\,P(D)=\dfrac{505}{882}\cdot\dfrac{882}{1441}=\dfrac{505}{1441} \approx 0.350$. The 882 cancels, just as the 734 did. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 c( direct_joint = mean(D & L), cond_on_late_times_base = mean(D[L]) * mean(L), cond_on_deal_times_base = mean(L[D]) * mean(D) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` direct_joint cond_on_late_times_base cond_on_deal_times_base 0.3504511 0.3504511 0.3504511 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ### The law of total probability

MIT explanation (review): 02.7 Total Probability Theorem.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 2 introduced a partition: events that do not overlap and together cover every outcome. The early seasons and the late seasons are a partition of the pitches. You can rebuild an overall probability from the parts of a partition in three steps. Take the conditional probability of $A$ within each part. Multiply it by the probability of that part, which gives a joint probability. Then add the joint probabilities. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Law of total probability.** For a partition $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ with every $P(B_i)>0$, $$P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(A\mid B_i)\,P(B_i).$$ In words: the overall probability of $A$ is a weighted average of its probabilities within the groups. The weight of each group is the probability of that group. ::: With only two groups, $B$ and its complement $B^c$, the sum has two terms: $$P(A)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)+P(A\mid B^c)\,P(B^c).$$ ::: {#exm-b04-total} ## Worked example: rebuilding P(D) from the deal rates of the two periods [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The early and late events $L^c$ and $L$ form a partition, so $$P(D)=P(D\mid L^c)\,P(L^c)+P(D\mid L)\,P(L) =\frac{377}{707}\cdot\frac{707}{1441} +\frac{505}{734}\cdot\frac{734}{1441} =\frac{377+505}{1441}=\frac{882}{1441}\approx 0.612.$$ Two kinds of number appear here. $377/707\approx 0.533$ and $505/734\approx 0.688$ are the deal rates within each period. $707/1441\approx 0.491$ and $734/1441\approx 0.509$ are the weights: the share of all pitches that falls in each period. The overall deal probability is a weighted average of the two rates. So it must lie between 0.533 and 0.688, and it is a little closer to the rate of the larger group. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 c( direct = mean(D), from_periods = mean(D[!L]) * mean(!L) + mean(D[L]) * mean(L) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` direct from_periods 0.6120749 0.6120749 ``` ::: ::: @fig-b04-partition-areas shows the same calculation as areas. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 p_early <- mean(!L) p_deal_early <- mean(D[!L]) p_deal_late <- mean(D[L]) ggplot() + # light backgrounds: the two parts of the partition annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = p_early, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.25) + annotate("rect", xmin = p_early, xmax = 1, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.25) + # solid areas: deal rate within each part, times the part's width annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = p_early, ymin = 0, ymax = p_deal_early, fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.85) + annotate("rect", xmin = p_early, xmax = 1, ymin = 0, ymax = p_deal_late, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.85) + annotate("segment", x = p_early, xend = p_early, y = 0, yend = 1, colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 1, ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = NA, colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = p_early / 2, y = 0.28, label = "D ~ symbol('\\307') ~ L^c", parse = TRUE, colour = "white", size = 4.2) + annotate("text", x = p_early + (1 - p_early) / 2, y = 0.36, label = "D ~ symbol('\\307') ~ L", parse = TRUE, colour = "white", size = 4.2) + annotate("text", x = p_early / 2, y = 0.88, label = "L^c", parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 4.4) + annotate("text", x = p_early + (1 - p_early) / 2, y = 0.88, label = "L", colour = "#17324D", size = 4.4) + annotate("text", x = 0.985, y = 0.955, label = "Omega", parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.8) + coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) + theme_void() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Total probability as areas. The two columns are the early and late seasons, a partition of all pitches. The width of a column is the probability of that period (the weight). The height of the solid region is the deal rate within that period. The two solid areas do not overlap, and their sum is P(D).](b04-conditioning-bayes-independence_files/figure-html/fig-b04-partition-areas-1.png){#fig-b04-partition-areas width=672} ::: ::: ### Bayes' rule: count first, formula second

MIT explanation (review): 02.8 Bayes' Rule.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Return to the prediction question from before class. An AI classifier reads the transcripts of pitches (the written text of what was said) and flags (marks) the pitches that it considers likely to reach a deal. Three numbers describe an invented classifier of this kind: - the **base rate**: 10% of the pitches that it checks reach a deal. - the **sensitivity**: among actual deals, 80% get flagged, $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})=0.80$. - the **false-positive rate**: among non-deals, 20% still get flagged, $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{no deal})=0.20$. A pitch has just been flagged. How likely is a deal now: near 80%, 50%, or 30%? Count first, and use the formula afterwards. ::: {#exm-b04-bayes-tree} ## Worked example: 1,000 imaginary pitches Imagine 1,000 pitches and apply the three numbers to them one after the other, as in @fig-b04-bayes-tree. 1. **Split by the base rate.** Of 1,000 pitches, 100 are deals and 900 are not. 2. **Flag the deals.** Sensitivity 80%: of the 100 deals, 80 are flagged. 3. **Flag some non-deals too.** False-positive rate 20%: of the 900 non-deals, 180 are flagged. 4. **Collect the flagged pitches.** In total $80+180=260$ pitches have a flag, and only 80 of them are deals: $$P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=\frac{80}{260}\approx 0.31.$$ The classifier finds 80% of deals, but fewer than a third of the flagged pitches are deals. The tree shows the reason. The 900 non-deals are a large group, so even a 20% false-positive rate produces 180 false flags. That is more than double the 80 true flags. A flag moves the deal probability from 10% to 31%. This is real evidence, but it is far from certainty. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"} old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)) plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.3, 9.7), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i") draw_node <- function(x, y, top, bottom, fill = "white", border = "#17324D", lwd = 1.4, w = 1.05, h = 0.78) { rect(x - w, y - h, x + w, y + h, col = fill, border = border, lwd = lwd) text(x, y + 0.26, top, font = 2, cex = 1.0, col = "#17324D") text(x, y - 0.30, bottom, cex = 0.8, col = "#5B6976") } draw_branch <- function(x1, y1, x2, y2, label, above = TRUE) { segments(x1, y1, x2, y2, col = "#9AA7B2", lwd = 1.6) text((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2 + if (above) 0.32 else -0.32, label, cex = 0.76, col = "#5B6976") } # branches first, then boxes on top draw_branch(2.45, 5.35, 3.55, 7.15, "10% deal") draw_branch(2.45, 4.65, 3.55, 2.85, "90% no deal", above = FALSE) draw_branch(5.65, 7.75, 6.95, 8.45, "80% flagged") draw_branch(5.65, 7.05, 6.95, 6.35, "20% not", above = FALSE) draw_branch(5.65, 2.95, 6.95, 3.65, "20% flagged") draw_branch(5.65, 2.25, 6.95, 1.55, "80% not", above = FALSE) draw_node(1.35, 5.0, "1,000", "pitches", w = 1.15) draw_node(4.6, 7.4, "100", "deal") draw_node(4.6, 2.6, "900", "no deal") draw_node(8.0, 8.6, "80", "flagged", fill = "#FDE5C1", border = "#D55E00", lwd = 2.2) draw_node(8.0, 6.2, "20", "not flagged", fill = "#F4F7F9", border = "#9AA7B2") draw_node(8.0, 3.8, "180", "flagged", fill = "#FDE5C1", border = "#D55E00", lwd = 2.2) draw_node(8.0, 1.4, "720", "not flagged", fill = "#F4F7F9", border = "#9AA7B2") text(9.55, 6.2, "260\nflagged\nin total", cex = 0.82, col = "#D55E00") par(old_par) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Tree of counts for 1,000 imaginary pitches. Orange boxes are the flagged pitches: 80 + 180 = 260 flags in total, of which only 80 are deals, so P(deal | flag) = 80/260, about 31%.](b04-conditioning-bayes-independence_files/figure-html/fig-b04-bayes-tree-1.png){#fig-b04-bayes-tree width=768} ::: ::: Now the formula. The question turns a condition around. We describe the quality of the classifier with $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})$, but the person who makes the decision needs $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})$. The multiplication rule gives the numerator, and the law of total probability gives the denominator. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Bayes' rule.** A formula that turns a conditional probability around: from $P(A\mid B)$ to $P(B\mid A)$. For events $A$ and $B$ with positive probability, $$P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}.$$ When $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ form a partition, you can write out the denominator $P(A)$ with the law of total probability: $$P(B_i\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_i)\,P(B_i)} {\sum_{j=1}^{k} P(A\mid B_j)\,P(B_j)}.$$ ::: For the classifier, the partition is deal and no deal: $$P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag}) =\frac{0.80\times 0.10}{0.80\times 0.10+0.20\times 0.90} =\frac{0.08}{0.08+0.18}=\frac{0.08}{0.26}\approx 0.308.$$ Every term is a branch of the tree, divided by 1,000: | Formula term | Value | Tree count | |---|---:|---| | $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})\,P(\text{deal})$ | $0.08$ | the 80 flagged deals | | $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{no deal})\,P(\text{no deal})$ | $0.18$ | the 180 flagged non-deals | | the denominator (total probability of a flag) | $0.26$ | all 260 flagged pitches | The formula is a short way to write the tree. Drawing a tree and counting is a good way to solve a Bayes question. Use an imaginary total that is easy to calculate with, such as 1,000. The tree and the formula always give the same answer. Bayes' rule also works on the Shark Tank events. Starting from $P(D\mid L)$, it gives $P(L\mid D)$: $$P(L\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid L)\,P(L)}{P(D)} =\frac{(505/734)(734/1441)}{882/1441}=\frac{505}{882}\approx 0.573.$$ The R check computes the same formula and compares it with the direct count from the table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 bayes_late_given_deal <- mean(D[L]) * mean(L) / mean(D) c( from_bayes = bayes_late_given_deal, from_table = mean(L[D]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` from_bayes from_table 0.5725624 0.5725624 ``` ::: ::: ### Independence of events

MIT explanation (review): 03.3 Independence of Two Events.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Sometimes knowing that one event happened tells you nothing about another event. Lecture 2 mentioned this idea. Conditional probability makes it precise. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Independent events.** Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when learning that $B$ happened does not change the probability of $A$. For $P(B)>0$, $$P(A\mid B)=P(A).$$ The same condition in **product form**: $$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B).$$ ::: The product form follows when you multiply both sides of the first equation by $P(B)$. It treats $A$ and $B$ in the same way, and it also works when an event has probability zero. Events that are not independent are called dependent. ::: {#exm-b04-independence} ## Worked example: are D and L independent? Check both forms with the numbers from the counts table. With conditioning: $P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688$, while $P(D)=882/1441\approx 0.612$. Learning that a pitch is late-season raises the deal probability, so $D$ and $L$ are not independent. With the product form: $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$, while $P(D)\,P(L)=\dfrac{882}{1441}\cdot\dfrac{734}{1441}\approx 0.612\times 0.509\approx 0.312$. The joint probability is larger than the product. This says the same thing: deals and late seasons occur together more often than they would under independence. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 L <- sharks$season >= 9 c( P_D_given_L = mean(D[L]), P_D = mean(D), P_D_and_L = mean(D & L), P_D_times_P_L = mean(D) * mean(L) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` P_D_given_L P_D P_D_and_L P_D_times_P_L 0.6880109 0.6120749 0.3504511 0.3117717 ``` ::: ::: **Disjoint is not independent.** Take the early and late events $L^c$ and $L$. They are disjoint: no pitch is in both periods, so $P(L^c\cap L)=0$. But the product $P(L^c)\,P(L)\approx 0.491\times 0.509\approx 0.25$ is not zero, so the product check fails. Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent. If you observe one of them, you know that the other did not happen. So one event tells you a lot about the other. ### Second application: deal rates by team composition [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The variable `pitcher_gender_group` in the Shark Tank file puts each team that pitches into one of four groups: `all_men`, `all_women`, `mixed`, or `unknown`. The deal rate within a category is a conditional probability, $P(D\mid \text{category})$, with the category as reference class. The code computes the three rates for the pitches with a known category: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1 known_gender <- sharks$pitcher_gender_group != "unknown" gender_labels <- c("all_men", "all_women", "mixed") gender_deal_rates <- tapply( sharks$deal_on_show[known_gender], factor(sharks$pitcher_gender_group[known_gender], levels = gender_labels), mean ) gender_deal_rates ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` all_men all_women mixed 0.5808538 0.6363636 0.6630435 They can still be compared, because each rate is a share within its own group. ::: {.caveat-box} What a conditional probability can and cannot say - Turning a condition around changes the number. Neither number shows a cause. 68.8% of late-season pitches got a deal. That does not mean that late seasons cause deals. - The team comparison uses the broad groups of presenters that the data source defined. It also uses only pitches that the producers selected. - The classifier numbers are invented for the example. **What you can do with it:** before you act on a signal, ask how often the outcome that you look for happens. With a low base rate, most signals are false alarms, so a cheap second check is worth its cost. ::: ### Answering the driving question The two sentences make different claims about the same 505 records. "68.8% of late-season pitches reached a deal" is $P(D\mid L)=505/734$, with the late seasons as reference class. "57.3% of deal pitches came from late seasons" is $P(L\mid D)=505/882$, with the deals as reference class. Both are correct. The typical error is to use the number of one sentence in the other. A positive flag from the AI classifier tells us less than its 80% sensitivity suggests. With a 10% base rate and a 20% false-positive rate, only $80/260\approx 31\%$ of flagged pitches are deals. The flag raises the probability of a deal from 10% to 31%, and not more. ::: {.founder-box} A founder's decision (invented example) Your venture sells boxes of prepared meals by subscription, and you give away free trial boxes. One in ten trial customers becomes a subscriber. You notice a signal: 80% of later subscribers open your follow-up email, and 20% of the others open it too. Count with 1,000 trial customers. 100 become subscribers, and 80 of them open the email. Of the other 900, 180 open it. So 80 of 260 openers become subscribers, about 31%. A phone call costs you 2 euros of time, and a subscriber is worth 30 euros. A call to an opener is worth 0.31 × 30 = 9.30 euros on average, so you call the openers. Among the 740 who did not open, only 20 become subscribers, under 3%. A call to one of them is worth about 0.80 euros on average. The decision: call the openers and nobody else. ::: **Next:** You can now update the probability of one event when another event is known. Lecture 5 looks at two random variables at the same time, for example the season of a pitch and the equity offered. It introduces two numbers that measure how two variables change together, the covariance and the correlation. It also shows what a correlation can and cannot tell you. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class After the lecture, work through all the practice below. ### Read the lecture material Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the most important parts. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly. ### Recall questions 1. What is the denominator of $P(A\mid B)$? 2. Why is $P(A\mid B)$ generally different from $P(B\mid A)$? 3. What makes a collection of events a partition? 4. What does the denominator in Bayes' rule calculate? 5. State the two equivalent definitions of independence of events. 6. Can two disjoint events, each with positive probability, be independent? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. $P(B)$, the probability of the conditioning event. 2. They condition on different reference classes, so they have different denominators. 3. No two parts overlap, and together they make up $\Omega$ (their union is $\Omega$). 4. The total probability of the observed evidence, added across all parts of the partition. 5. $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ (learning $B$ does not change the probability of $A$), and the product form $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)$. 6. No. Their intersection has probability 0 while the product of their probabilities is positive, so the product check fails. Observing one makes the other impossible. ::: ### Finish a half-worked example: the Bayes tree Re-read the worked example with the tree of 1,000 pitches (@exm-b04-bayes-tree). Then build the tree again with new numbers: base rate 20%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 30%. *Step 1 (given).* Start with 1,000 imaginary pitches: 200 deals, 800 non-deals. *Step 2 (you).* Fill in the four boxes at the end of the tree: the flagged and the unflagged counts in each branch. *Step 3 (you).* Collect the flagged pitches and compute $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Of the 200 deals, 90% are flagged: 180. Of the 800 non-deals, 30% are flagged: 240. Flagged total $180+240=420$, of which 180 are deals: $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=180/420\approx 0.429$. The formula agrees: $\dfrac{0.90\times 0.20}{0.90\times 0.20+0.30\times 0.80} =\dfrac{0.18}{0.42}\approx 0.429$. ::: **On your own.** A stricter classifier checks a group of pitches in which 5% reach a deal. Its sensitivity is 90% and its false-positive rate is 10%. What share of flagged pitches are deals? Use either the tree or the formula. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer With 1,000 pitches: 50 deals, of which 45 are flagged, and 950 non-deals, of which 95 are flagged. $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=45/(45+95)=45/140\approx 0.321$. Even with 90% sensitivity and a low false-positive rate, the 5% base rate keeps the share of true flags below one third. ::: ### Practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the counts table: 330, 229, 377, 505, with totals 559, 882, 707, 734, and 1,441. 1. Use the early/late partition to verify $P(D)=P(D\mid L^c)\,P(L^c)+P(D\mid L)\,P(L)$. 2. Calculate and interpret $P(L\mid D)$. Explain why it differs from $P(D\mid L)$. 3. Decide by calculation whether $D$ and $L$ are independent, using the product form. 4. The events $L^c$ and $L$ are disjoint. Are they independent? Explain in one sentence. 5. Consider the 1,434 pitches with a known classification of the team. Of the 661 pitches with women represented (all-women or mixed), 428 reached an on-air deal. Of the 773 all-men pitches, 449 reached an on-air deal. Calculate both conditional deal proportions and interpret the difference. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. $(377/707)(707/1441)+(505/734)(734/1441)=(377+505)/1441=882/1441 \approx 0.612$. 2. $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 0.573$: among deal records, 57.3% came from Seasons 9--16. It differs from $P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688$ because the conditioning event, and so the denominator, is different. 3. $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$, while $P(D)\,P(L)=(882/1441)(734/1441)\approx 0.312$. The two are not equal, so $D$ and $L$ are not independent. 4. No: $P(L^c\cap L)=0$ but $P(L^c)\,P(L)\approx 0.25>0$, so the product check fails. Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent. 5. $428/661\approx 0.648$ and $449/773\approx 0.581$, a descriptive difference of about 6.7 percentage points. The data source defined the groups, and the producers chose the pitches for television. The difference does not show that the kind of team causes the deal. ::: ### Review: one question from Lecture 3 A variable $Y$ has PMF $p_Y(0)=0.2$, $p_Y(1)=0.5$, and $p_Y(2)=0.3$. Calculate $E[Y]$ and say in one sentence what the number means. Can $Y$ ever equal it exactly? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer $E[Y]=0(0.2)+1(0.5)+2(0.3)=1.1$. It is the probability-weighted average of the possible values, and the long-run average over many repetitions. It does not have to be a value that the variable can take: here $Y$ is never 1.1. ::: ### Worked exam interpretation [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Question.** A student sees $P(D\mid L)=0.688$ and writes, "68.8% of deal pitches came from late seasons." Explain what is wrong and give the correct interpretation. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer The calculation conditions on $L$, so the denominator is the 734 pitches in Seasons 9--16. The correct interpretation is that 68.8% of late-season records reached an on-air deal. The sentence the student wrote describes the reversed conditional probability, $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 57.3\%$.
